# Figures

![**Conceptual workflow figure for data preparation and quantification of the relative importance of past humans and climate on variability in PAPs at different spatial and temporal scales.** From left to right, the main sources of proxy data (Sources (proxies)), what variables are derived from the data (Variables), what they can infer (Inference), data aggregation (Spatial units), the models of the hierarchical variation partitioning analyses and attribution (HVARPART analysis), and the quantification of the ratios of predictor importance between past humans and climate (Predictor importance (ratios)) are shown. See **Methods** for more detailed explanations. Data summaries of fossil pollen sequences, radiocarbon dates, and human-impact events are shown in [@extfig-data-coverage; @extfig-human-data-coverage]. Two site-based examples of quantification of predictor importance between past humans and climate combined are shown in @extfig-site-examples. The general predictor trends of past humans in different climate zones for each continental region are shown in @extfig-spd-trajectories, and the palaeoclimate represented by mean annual temperature (MAT ℃), minimum temperature of the coldest month (Cold ℃), precipitation of warmest quarter (Summer prec), and precipitation of coldest quarter (Winter prec) for different climate zones are shown in [@extfig-annual-temperature; @extfig-coldest-month-temperature; @extfig-warmest-quarter-precipitation; @extfig-coldest-quarter-precipitation]. The general trends for human-impact events in different climate zones are shown in @extfig-human-events.](figures/figure-01-conceptual-workflow.png){#fig-conceptual-workflow width=100% fig-alt="Conceptual workflow linking proxy sources, derived variables, spatial units, HVARPART models, and predictor-importance ratios."}

![**Ratios of predictor importance of past humans and palaeoclimate on variability in PAPs over the period of 8.5-2 ka BP across climate zones and continents.** Each row represents a continent: North America, Central and South America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania. The colours represent Köppen-Geiger climate zones[@main-ref-36]. Panel A shows the spatial distribution of individual sequences represented by coloured dots on the regional maps (Number of sequences listed in @tbl-pap-metrics; @extfig-data-coverage). Note that we are only showing the parts of the map with sequences. Panel B shows the regional density curves of the distribution of human importance ratios within a continent (colour gold). Panel C shows the weighted mean ratios of importance (y-axis) of past humans summarised at the level of continents (horizontal gold line) and climate zones (circles). Panel D shows the regional density curves of the distribution of palaeoclimatic importance ratios within a continent (colour teal). Panel E shows the weighted mean ratios of importance (y-axis) of palaeoclimate (colour teal) at the level of continents (horizontal teal line) and climate zones (circles). For each climate zone, the different shading and width of the lines are the percentile ranges (50<sup>th</sup>, 75<sup>th</sup>, and 95<sup>th</sup>) of individual ratios per sequence. Only climate zones with \> 2 sequences are used in this visualisation.](figures/figure-02-predictor-importance-spatial.png){#fig-predictor-importance-spatial width=100% fig-alt="Maps and density plots comparing human and climate importance across continents and climate zones."}

![**Ratios of predictor importance of past humans (summed probability density (SPD) and Human-Impact Events) to palaeoclimate on variability in PAPs within time slices for each continent.** The bar charts show the ratios of importance between past humans (Humans (SPD)) and palaeoclimate (Climate) as predictors (dark green and gold shaded bars), and the ratios of importance between human-impact events (Humans (Events)) and palaeoclimate (Climate) predictors (dark green and red-brown shaded bars) for the hierarchical variation partitioning (HVARPART). The human-impact events cover additional time slices from 2.0–0.5 ka BP where SPDs are lacking. The ratio of importance (y-axis) varies from 0 to 1.](figures/figure-03-predictor-importance-temporal.png){#fig-predictor-importance-temporal width=100% fig-alt="Stacked bars comparing human and climate predictor importance through time for five continents."}

![**Ratios of importance of past humans in relation to palaeoclimate in influencing the interrelationships among PAPs in different climate zones across the continents.** Each row represents a continental region as follows: North America, Central and South America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania. The columns from left to right represent a total of 11 climate zones within the main Polar, Cold, Temperate, Tropical, and Arid zones. The left bar charts represent the ratios of predictor importance of past human presence (gold) in relation to climate (teal) for changes in the relationships among PAPs for the period 8.5–2 ka BP (y-axis on a scale 0–1). The spread in time trajectories in the ordination space (grey circles) indicates the total amount of change in the interrelationships between PAPs in different time slices, and the ordination space is scaled to similar units to allow comparison across climate zones and continents. The sample scores of the distance-based redundancy analysis (dbRDA) in hierarchical variation partitioning (HVARPART) are plotted as time trajectories (blue lines). These trajectories show the direction of change, where it starts at 8.5 ka BP (dark blue) and progresses towards 2 ka BP (light blue). Arrows, indicating past human presence (gold) and palaeoclimatic variables (teal), show the influence of each predictor over time on the interrelationship among PAPs. The direction of the arrows indicates the trend of influence, while their length quantifies the strength of association between predictors and changes in interrelationships among PAPs, with longer arrows representing stronger influences.](figures/figure-04-pap-interrelationships.png){#fig-pap-interrelationships width=100% fig-alt="Ordination trajectories and predictor arrows for PAP interrelationships across climate zones and continents."}
